speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry (a) whether he can provide an update on industry transformation plans for the marine and offshore engineering (M&OE) sector; and (b) whether the Industry Transformation Maps and related policy reviews have considered what opportunities may exist in offshore carrier transport of hydrogen.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Climate change is an existential challenge for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Are you taking Question Nos 3 to 5 together?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I know this is the second time you have reminded me in two days.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: So, it is a combined response to Question Nos 3 to 5?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I was vacillating between sustainable jobs and sustainable energy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Climate change is an existential challenge for Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: One of our key thrusts under LEDS is to adopt advanced low-carbon technologies, such as carbon capture, utilisation and storage, or CCUS, and low-carbon hydrogen, to decarbonise our economy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For CCUS, a small number of pathways are at a technologically advanced stage, but it requires further development to be commercially viable in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: A key pathway is carbon capture and storage, or CCS.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are seeing more large-scale projects being developed with government support internationally.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This includes Project Longship1 and PORTHOS2 in Norway and the Netherlands respectively.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, Singapore faces challenges in deploying CCS domestically, including a lack of any known geological formations that are suitable for the permanent storage of carbon dioxide underground.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are, therefore, exploring partnerships with companies and other countries with suitable geological formations to enable carbon dioxide storage opportunities.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are also exploring carbon capture and utilisation (CCU) pathways, where carbon dioxide is captured and converted into waste-based feedstocks or natural minerals that can be used to produce aggregates for reclamation or building materials in the form of building materials.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There are a number of companies developing testbeds for use in Singapore and examples of commercial-scale operations in other countries.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Captured carbon dioxide may also be used to manufacture synthetic fuels and chemicals, such as kerosene and methanol, which can be used as aviation and marine fuels.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, most pathways for synthesising fuels or chemicals from carbon dioxide are not mature and they are relatively nascent.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Though some are at demonstration or post-demonstration stage, they can be expensive compared to conventional production, while others remain at scales that are still within the lab; so, it is still at lab-scale.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Some also require significant amounts of energy in the form of low-carbon hydrogen, which will take some time to become cost-competitive with other conventional sources of energy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Low-carbon hydrogen is a key technology for Singapore to decarbonise.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: A recent feasibility study commissioned by Government agencies and published in June this year concluded that hydrogen has the potential to decarbonise maritime, electricity generation, heavy transportation and some industrial processes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, until CCUS is commercially viable, Singapore cannot produce low-carbon hydrogen at scale.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Hence, we are exploring a range of other supply pathways.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The key challenge with scaling up the supply of hydrogen is the very high storage and transportation costs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Hydrogen, as most of you would know, is a gas with a boiling point far lower than natural gas.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is, therefore, a significant engineering challenge to transport and to store hydrogen in a commercially viable manner.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To overcome this problem, the industry is working on different hydrogen carriers, each with its advantages, but also with its challenges to overcome.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Supply chains exist today for ammonia, but ammonia is currently not produced using low-carbon methods or shipped in quantities required of an energy carrier.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To avoid this, we need to first liberate the hydrogen in ammonia, which would require a lot of energy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, it is, by itself, an energy-intensive process.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Liquid Organic Hydride Carriers (LOHCs), which allow storage and transport of hydrogen at ambient conditions, are less hydrogen-dense, but this means a relatively higher cargo footprint would be needed to import the same amount of hydrogen.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The process required to release hydrogen from these LOHCs can also be land- and energy-intensive.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The third form, liquefied hydrogen, is where hydrogen is transported in its natural form.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The process to liquify hydrogen for transport is, again, very energy-intensive and the technology for the large-scale shipping of liquefied hydrogen is relatively nascent today.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There is currently no global consensus on which carrier form of hydrogen might dominate in the future, or when long-distance transport of hydrogen and the processes to liberate hydrogen from carriers might become viable.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Singapore is keen to realise the decarbonisation potential of hydrogen and to develop into a regional hydrogen hub.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Government agencies will continue to monitor the technological and market developments to ensure that Singapore maintains its competitiveness.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Additionally, we will continue to collaborate with companies and the research community on Research, Development and Demonstration (RD&D) projects and testbeds for CCUS solutions as well as low-carbon hydrogen.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We look forward to more partnerships and to leveraging them to capture new opportunities from emerging technologies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng also asked specifically about the Industry Transformation Map (ITM) of the marine and offshore engineering (M&OE) sector.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And if I may sustain a couple of supplementary questions as well on this issue.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On the first point, the Minister spoke about how there are currently significant constraints regarding the deployment of clean hydrogen and its transport.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some of these constraints appear to be specific to the origin, as well as the destination – the liquefaction and then the subsequent gasification at the destination.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: However, I would like to ask the Minister whether he sees, at some point, opportunities arising further in the transport of liquid hydrogen.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I understand that there are some prototype developments from the Japanese in this sector and even as we explore opportunities for the Offshore and Marine Engineering sector, I wonder if the Ministry is looking at ways to keep our industry ready in the event that some of these new modalities and technologies start to become commercially viable.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: How will these developments he has outlined maintain Singapore's competitiveness and access to markets around the world?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With regard to the opportunities arising from the transport of hydrogen, certainly, we do not rest on our laurels.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If anything, given how we have gone through the last many decades, first, as a petrochemical, oil and gas centre of excellence for the last five decades, as we pivot into sustainable fuels into a low-carbon emission strategy, we envisaged that our strategic hub status we will continue to pivot.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will continue to leverage on what we have built thus far to become the crossroads once the transportation of liquid hydrogen or, for that matter, even in the trading of electrons, electricity.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We can envisage that it is one market that we think we can leverage and become the hub in this entire region.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Certainly, it is one of those initiatives that we are driving and actively looking at.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Today, a number of technologies are quite nascent, even though they hold a lot of promise.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There is option value in exploring and studying which is the likely initiative that is going to give us maximum benefit and maximum economic value.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, it is one of those things where we look at the myriad of opportunities that are available, the research and development, and we are plugged into many of these research initiatives; and once we are able to land and the vision gets clearer in terms of where each one of these technologies is moving, I think we will be able to leverage and extract the synergies that can help move us ahead.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With regard to the changing environment and the access to markets, if you look at where we are, how we are pivoting our entire oil and gas sector, we are looking at more sustainable development in terms of the fuels that we are in.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Two big companies have come and invested in our country.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are now looking at the production of sustainable aviation fuels as well, although, again, the technology is relatively nascent.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It costs a lot more to pivot from existing fuels and natural gases to go into sustainable aviation fuel, but it is one of those things that we cannot ignore as well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There are separate initiatives that drive that part of it.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With regard to hydrogen today, it is very difficult and it is very, very expensive and it is not very productive, not very efficient for us to produce green hydrogen, which is the cleanest form of hydrogen in Singapore, because we are geographically disadvantaged.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These are various initiatives that we are looking at and I take Dr Tan Wu Meng's point to heart.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will actively seek out the best, the most cost-effective way, whilst taking into consideration our NDC commitment targets to establish ourselves as a hub in this region.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Could I just ask, with these new exciting developments in hydrogen and CCUS, if they do become feasible, whether we are also then reviewing our projections on when we can reach net zero emissions?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, if hydrogen CCUS becomes visible, maybe can we reach net zero by 2050?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have every intention of reaching the target within the second half of this century.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If we are able to bring it forward, that would be really an added bonus and it is something that we always will aspire to do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I just wonder if I could follow up.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: He mentioned that one of the important objectives is demonstration projects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We know that one element of demonstration projects that have been rolled out in many countries around the world is hydrogen in the form of public transportation, especially buses and taxicabs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am keenly aware of the negative demonstration example of cases like the Hindenburg, but I wonder, especially when we are looking to transition our fleet beyond just electricity to a low carbon future, whether this will be part of the push in terms of our public transportation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I mentioned this earlier in my reply to Dr Tan Wu Meng's Parliamentary Questions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is co-driven by EDB and EMA with A*STAR as the implementing agency on behalf of the Government.
